124-deuterocanonical-books-of-the-bible-:
Some Bibles include books that others set apart, and this volume gathers them. The Deuterocanonical Books, also called the Apocrypha, include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, and Baruch. Esdras, the additions to Esther and Daniel, and the Maccabees books appear as well.

These writings come from the centuries between the Testaments, in Greek and Hebrew traditions. They tell of exiles, martyrs, wise sayings, and revolts for the faith. Churches differ on their authority, but all value their history. The collection gives readers the full disputed shelf in one place. Study notes in many editions explain where each book fits in Jewish and Christian history.
15571-mary-cary-frequently-martha:
Kate Langley Bosher published this novel in 1910, with Harper and Brothers, in a Grosset and Dunlap edition, with a frontispiece by Frances Rogers. It is told by Mary Cary herself, an orphan at the Yorkburg Female Orphan Asylum, who insists that things do happen in an orphan asylum. Orphans, she says, are real children, much like children with mothers and fathers, though they give no parties and wear no truly Paris clothes.

Fifteen chapters follow Mary from an unthankful orphan through the coming of Miss Katherine, the stepped-on and the steppers, a Reagan ball, and a true miracle, to a real wedding. The title chapter, Mary, Frequently Martha, names her busy, serving spirit. Bosher writes a warm, funny story of a girl who learns gratitude and love, in a voice that young readers still find direct and winning.
16296-sketches-from-my-life-by-the-late-:
Admiral Hobart Pasha set down these memories near the end of his life, and friends put them in print after his death in 1887. The book moves from a rough start at sea to slave hunting off Africa, blockade running, a visit to Charleston, and the siege of Richmond. Later chapters follow him into the Turkish navy, the war with Russia, and sport in Turkey.

Much of it was dictated on the Riviera while he was ill, and the tone stays plain and frank throughout. He names ships and ports, recalls close calls, and sketches the men he served with. For readers who like sea tales told by a man who lived them, the book gives a full naval life in short, brisk chapters.
17451-sign-language-among-north-american:
Garrick Mallery wrote this comparative study of sign language among North American Indians, set beside that of other peoples and of deaf mutes. Its long list of pictures shows signs for affirmation and approbation in old Roman, Neapolitan, and North American Indian use, for negation in Dakota use, and for love in modern Neapolitan use. Groups, questions, thieves, marriages, and money all appear among the illustrated signs.

Readers get a pioneering work of gesture studies, arguing that sign systems across cultures can be compared like spoken tongues. Mallery's plates make the argument visible, sign by sign. The book remains a foundation text for the study of gesture and of Indian sign language.
18822-the-house-of-martha:
Frank R. Stockton published this novel with Houghton, Mifflin in 1891. Its narrator, an only grandchild raised by his grandmother, tells his story from her quiet village house. From her parlor window she watches the street, trusting that he always does what is right.

Chapters follow his year in Europe, his book of travel, and a Sicilian love story, with a listener, an under-study, and a plan of seclusion along the way. Genoa, a sandbar, a floating grocery, and a distant topsail mark his wanderings, while Tomaso, Lucilla, and Sylvia people his tale. Stockton mixes gentle humor with romance, letting a traveler's book grow out of meetings, letters, and unfinished work.
19-the-song-of-hiawatha:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow built an American epic from Ojibway legends gathered by Henry Rowe Schoolcraft. The Song of Hiawatha follows its hero from childhood to farewell in twenty-two cantos. Its steady trochaic beat made it easy to recite and remember.

Hiawatha learns the ways of forest and water, woos Minnehaha, and faces famine and loss. Chapters cover fasting, fishing, sailing, picture-writing, and the coming of white men. The poem closes with his departure as a new age arrives. Its popularity shaped how generations pictured Native stories, for better and worse.
24917-mariucha:
Benito Perez Galdos wrote Mariucha, a comedy in five acts, in this school edition prepared by S. Griswold Morley for Heath's Modern Language Series in 1921. The Spanish text comes with an introduction, notes, and a vocabulary for students.

Morley's life of Galdos notes that the author was born at Las Palmas in 1843. He studied law at Madrid without liking it, and turned from failed stage plays to novels before returning to drama. In Mariucha, Maria faces shame over letters her father, the Marques, pressed her to write in his straitened state. The edition suits students reading classic Spanish drama in the original.
26774-alcohol-a-dangerous-and-unnecessar:
Mrs. Martha M. Allen, superintendent of the Department of Medical Temperance for the National Woman's Christian Temperance Union, published this temperance book at Marcellus, New York, in 1900. Its subtitle promises how and why, with what medical writers say. Allen argues that alcohol is a dangerous and unnecessary medicine, and gathers doctors' opinions written in response to her letters of inquiry.

Chapters treat the Woman's Christian Temperance Union against alcohol as medicine, alcohol as a producer of disease, temperance hospitals, and the effects of alcohol upon the human body. Later chapters cover alcohol as medicine, alcohol in pharmacy, diseases and their treatment without alcohol, and alcohol and nursing mothers. Doctors quoted condemn alcohol for tubercular patients, saying it lowers resistance and leaves the person more open to disease.
27299-nothing-to-say-a-slight-slap-at-mo:
Nothing to Say, a slight slap at mobocratic snobbery, belongs to the Doesticks books, advertised as the funniest works in existence from Rudd and Carleton. The volume gathers the satires of Q. K. Philander Doesticks, Perfect Brick, whose letters were copied, quoted, and laughed over wherever they were lent.

Companion titles include Doesticks, What He Says, the compilation of his original letters, Plu-ri-bus-tah, a song by no author, and The Elephant Club, by Doesticks and Knight Russ Ockside. The verse spares neither the spirit of cant nor popular humbug and vulgar rant, in mid-century American comic satire.
32426-a-synopsis-of-the-north-american-l:
E. Raymond Hall's Synopsis of the North American Lagomorpha surveys rabbits, hares, and pikas of North America. It was published by the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History in volume five, number ten, pages 119 to 202, on December 15, 1951. With sixty-eight figures in the text, the synopsis gives the systematic treatment specialists need: names, ranges, characters, and relationships among lagomorph groups.

Hall, chairman of the museum's editorial committee, wrote for a series exchanged with learned societies, universities, and libraries. The paper's Latin-1 text marks male and female symbols and preserves bold, italic, and small-cap type from the original. It remains a standard reference for mammalogists studying North American lagomorph taxonomy and distribution.
8213-three-years-in-tristan-da-cunha:
K. M. Barrow, wife of the Reverend J. G. Barrow, missionary clergyman on Tristan da Cunha, wrote this account of three years on the remotest inhabited island in the world. With thirty-seven original illustrations from photographs and a map. The book aims to give a simple and true description of daily life among a very small community cut off from the rest of the world. Its language is largely that of letters to a sister and of Barrow's journal, with use of the official Blue Book and the Africa Pilot.

Barrow describes island routines, storms, ships, births, and burials, without literary pretence. The result is an intimate record of isolation and community. For readers of travel and island life, it is a rare, first-hand portrait of Tristan before modern communications, told by a woman who lived it.
8324-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-24-cant:
Lovers speak, seek, and find each other in the Canticle of Canticles, the Douay-Rheims name for the Song of Songs. A young woman and her beloved praise each other's beauty in images from vineyards, gardens, spices, and the hills of Lebanon, parting and reuniting in verses of longing. No plot holds the poems together, only desire and delight.

Jewish tradition reads the song for Passover, and Christians have read it as Christ's love for the church, but the poems also stand as plain love poetry. Challoner's revision from the Latin Vulgate gives the verses in older Catholic wording, with the Latin title kept. It is the Bible's most sensual book, and one of its shortest.
ayesha:
H. Rider Haggard brought back his deathless queen Ayesha in this book of 1905. Its full name is Ayesha: The Return of She. Fans had waited near twenty years since She first came out to learn her fate. Leo's quest, and hers, had held readers since that first wild book.

Leo Vincey, who loved Ayesha in the first book, is drawn to her new form in the hills of Asia. The tale ranges through storms, cults, and the fire of her strange rebirth in full stretch. Haggard gives his occult romance its most vast and wild form in this long tale.
britannica-1911-agrapha:
Agrapha means unwritten things in Greek. The name covers sayings ascribed to Jesus outside the Gospels. Such utterances survive in other early documents. Acts quotes one: it is more blessed to give than receive. Paul's letters preserve several more sayings. The Logia found at Oxyrhynchus in 1897 joined them. Those papyrus finds renewed scholarly interest greatly. Two examples show the range of material.

One saying promises the weak salvation through the strong. It comes from the Apostolic Canons, about A.D. 300. The second calls the world merely a bridge. Cross over it, it says, do not dwell on it. Missionary Alexander Duff found that saying in Arabic. It was inscribed on a mosque gateway at Fatehpur Sikri. Collections began with Cotelerius in the seventeenth century.
britannica-1911-ahmed-tewfik-pasha:
Ahmed Tewfik Pasha, a Turkish diplomat born in 1845, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Ismail Hakki Pasha. He began his career in the army, then left the service in 1862 while still a young man. Four years later he entered diplomacy instead, and was employed at various European capitals.

Steady postings carried him upward through the Ottoman foreign service. He became minister at Athens in 1883, the empire's resident envoy to Greece. The next year he rose to ambassador in Berlin, one of the great postings of the day. In 1896 he reached the top of his profession at home. He was appointed minister for foreign affairs, the office the entry gives in Turkish as Kharijie Naziri.
britannica-1911-ali-pasha:
Ali Pasha (1741–1822), the Turkish ruler of Iannina nicknamed Arslan, the Lion, grew up bent on revenge. He was born at Tepeleni, an Albanian village below the Klissura mountains, into a Toske family. His forebears, hereditary beys of the place, lost their lands after nearby chiefs slew his father.

His mother Khamko, a woman of strong character, raised and led a band of brigands herself. She trained her son in her own fierce spirit, aiming him at payback and at winning back the lost estate. Ali learned fast. Scores of tales praise the cunning he showed as a young brigand chief in the hills. By a bold trick he seized Tepeleni again and settled scores with his foes. The long entry then tracks his years of rule and the struggle for Parga, which its people gave to the British in 1814 rather than let him take it.
britannica-1911-batalha:
Batalha, a town of Portugal in the district of Leiria, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a place known for one great building. The town, with 3858 people in 1900, stands on the site of old Canoeira. Its name, the Portuguese word for battle, and the monastery's name both recall the fight at Aljubarrota in 1385. There John I of Portugal beat John I of Castile and kept his kingdom free.

Dominicans built the monastery of Santa Maria da Victoria, St Mary of the Victory, in golden-brown stone cut like marble. It runs about 500 feet from north to south. Inside are a royal cloister, a chapter-house, and the Founder's chapel. That chapel holds the tombs of John I, Queen Philippa, and Prince Henry the Navigator. Kings after them lie in the round royal tomb house, famed for fine carved stone.
britannica-1911-buddha:
Buddha is the title given to the founder of Buddhism. In Europe the name means the last historical Buddha. His family name was Gotama. This long 1911 Britannica article examines his life. He was the son of Suddhodana, a chief of the Sakiya clan. That clan was one of India's republican tribes.

The article opens with a warning about legend. Miraculous tales gather around every religious founder, it says. Some scholars once called the Buddha a pure myth. The entry rejects that view firmly. A basis of truth lies under the tales, it argues. The article then sets out his birth and early circumstances. It places them in the 6th century B.C. It weighs the oldest records against the later legends. Its aim is an intelligent history of the man. Readers get both the tradition and the criticism of it.
britannica-1911-chickasha:
Chickasha is a city and the county-seat of Grady county, Oklahoma, near the Washita river, about 45 miles south-south-west of Oklahoma City. Its people rose from 3,209 in 1900 to 10,320 in 1910, a fast growth in a new state. Three railways serve the city, the St Louis and San Francisco, the Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific and the Oklahoma Central. The city is the trade centre of a very fertile part of the Washita Valley.

Corn, cotton, fruits, vegetables and live-stock are the chief products of that valley land. Manufactures in the city include flour, cotton-seed oil, lumber, furniture and farm implements. Chickasha was founded in 1892, only seven years before it was chartered as a city in 1899. Fertile soil, rail links and new town growth explain the sharp rise in numbers that the entry records.
britannica-1911-covilha:
Covilhã is a town of Portugal in the district of Castello Branco, once part of the province of Beira. It stands on the east slope of the Serra da Estrella, on the Abrantes to Guarda railway. Its people numbered 15,469 in 1900. The town has often been likened to a clutch of swallows' nests. Those nests cling to a rugged granite mountain side in the image.

Houses crowd in the shape of an amphitheatre on that slope. They look down on the river Zezere and its wild valley from 2,180 feet. More than 4,000 workers make saragoça in the town. That coarse brown cloth is worn by the peasantry across Portugal. The village of Unhaes da Serra lies six miles west. Its sulphur springs and baths draw note in the entry. Cloth, height and springs form the town's whole mark.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agrapha:
Agrapha, a name J. G. Korner first used in 1776 for Jesus's Sayings surviving outside the canonical Gospels. After Alfred Resch chose the expression as his learned work's title on these Sayings in 1889, its technical meaning was generally accepted. The entry considers the Agrapha's limits first, their genuineness criteria second, and the list of those probably authentic.

Three conditions govern the Agrapha. They must be Sayings, not discourses; Sayings of Jesus; and not contained in the canonical Gospels. Being mere Sayings, they exclude long Jesus sections in the Didascalia and Pistis Sophia. Being Sayings of Jesus, they exclude sayings in religious romances such as apocryphal Gospels and Acts or Christ's Letter to Abgar. They also exclude Scripture passages ascribed to Jesus by mere oversight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocrypha:
Apocrypha covers writings that claim authorship by biblical figures, and this long article sorts them by origin rather than by the misleading split into Old and New Testament groups. Works once called apocryphal but now counted as patristic literature, such as the Shepherd of Hermas, the Letter of Barnabas, and the Didache are treated elsewhere. Jewish apocrypha broadly match the Old Testament set, and Christian apocrypha the New Testament set.

The survey runs through Jewish apocalypses, legendary tales, psalms and prayers, and philosophy. Then it covers Jewish works with Christian additions, then Christian gospels, Pilate literature, acts of apostles, doctrinal works, epistles, and apocalypses. The entry is a map for readers who meet a strange gospel or lost psalm. It shows where it came from, when it was written, and why it never entered the canon, the accepted list of Scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bertha:
Bertha, a name borne by several holy women, receives a grouped entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, with five singled out for notice. First stands Bertha, Queen of Kent, a Frankish princess who married the pagan King Ethelbert and brought her chaplain Liudhard to Canterbury. There she restored a Roman-era church dedicated to St. Martin.

Her influence smoothed the way for St. Augustine's mission of 596, and Pope Gregory wrote to her in 601. Other Berthas in the entry include abbesses and queens of later centuries. The piece is a small gallery of women who carried faith into courts and convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-birtha:
Birtha, a titular see of Osrhoene, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Probably the same as Birejik on the Euphrates, some sixty-two miles west of Edessa, its Aramaic name means castle, and ancient writers call it just that. A second name, Macedonopolis, claims Alexander the Great as founder by legend.

Proof that Birtha and Macedonopolis are one see comes from Nicaea's subscription lists, where the Syriac and Arabic form matches the Greek and Latin name. The entry is a short identification puzzle solved by comparing council lists across languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-kateri-tek:
Blessed Kateri Tekakwitha, the Lily of the Mohawks, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1656 at Ossernenon or Gandaouge, she died at Caughnawaga in Canada in 1680. Her mother was a Christian Algonquin captured by the Iroquois, saved by Tekakwitha's father, and mother also of a son.

Smallpox at about four killed her parents and brother, and aunts and a chief uncle adopted her. Baptised despite family opposition, she lived a life of prayer and penance, fleeing to the Christian village of Caughnawaga. The entry presents a young Mohawk woman whose holiness bridged two worlds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canatha:
Canatha was a titular see of Arabia, named Kanatha, Kanotha, or even Kenetha on coins and in geographies, with its own era. It is certainly not Kanata, now Kerak, nor Maximianopolis, since Severus of that see and Theodosius of Kenatha sat together at Chalcedon in 451. Josephus first mentions it for a defeat of Herod by the Arabs, and Pliny and Ptolemy count it among the towns of the Decapolis.

In the old episcopal lists it answers to Bostra as suffragan, and one bishop is known, Theodosius, from 449 to 458. Today it is El-Qanawat, northeast of Bostra at about 4,100 feet, amid woods. Its magnificent ruins run 4,800 feet long, among them a Roman bridge, a rock-hewn theatre, a nymphaeum, an aqueduct, and two temples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eliseus-elish:
Eliseus, or Elisha, was the prophet who followed Elijah, and this entry follows his wonder-working career. On Mount Horeb, Elijah learned that Elisha son of Shaphat was chosen as his successor. Elijah cast his mantle over Elisha as he ploughed with twelve yoke of oxen. Elisha killed the oxen, boiled their flesh on his plough wood, feasted with family and friends, and then followed his master.

After Elijah was taken up in a fiery chariot, Elisha parted the Jordan with the fallen mantle and won recognition at Jericho as heir to Elijah's spirit. He healed Jericho's waters with salt, and bears mauled boys who mocked him at Bethel. Later he multiplied a widow's oil to pay her debt, and he foretold both rain and victory for the allied kings against Moab. The entry shows a prophet whose miracles served the poor, the king, and the nation alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fray-antonio-:
Fray Antonio de la Calancha, an erudite Augustinian monk born in 1584 at Chuquisaca, now Sucre, in Bolivia, and dead on 1 March 1654. He wrote one of the great chronicles of colonial Peru. Both his parents were of Spanish blood, he studied at Lima, entered the Order of St. Augustine, and served successively as definitor, secretary of the province, and rector of the College of San Ildefonso. During the earthquake that ravaged Trujillo on 14 February 1619 he headed that city's convent, and later became prior at Lima.

His most important work, the Moralised Chronicle of the Order of St. Augustine in Peru, appeared in two bulky volumes in 1638 and 1653, now very rare, written in a ponderous style but full of valuable detail on the Indians of Peru and Bolivia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabbatha:
Gabbatha is the Aramaic name for the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat in judgment on Jesus. It appears only in John 19:13, beside the Greek name Lithostrotos. John calls the tongue Hebrew, as New Testament writers did, though the speech of Judea in that day was Aramaic. The entry weighs what the two names truly mean.

Lithostrotos means a mosaic pavement, the floor before Pilate's headquarters where his judgment seat stood. Gabbatha, by contrast, comes from a root meaning back or height, pointing to the rise of the ground itself. Scholars have tried to pin the spot to the Temple court, the Sanhedrin's meeting place, or a ridge behind the Temple, but none of these guesses holds. Only Pilate's seat there stands certain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerrha:
Gerrha, a titular see in Augustamnica Prima suffragan of Pelusium under Alexandria, survives in geographers and bishops' lists. Pliny mentions the city, Eratosthenes says its district once lay underwater, and Strabo sets it between Pelusium and Mount Cassius. Hierocles in the sixth century places it in Augustamnica.

Lequien gives four bishops: Eudaemon, Pirosus, and Nilanmon at the fourth century's end and the fifth's start, and Stephen, who attended Chalcedon in 451. Marshes have since encroached on the land, and the abandoned city lies on the El-Arish road north of Pelusium. The entry's brevity suits readers tracing Egypt's lesser sees, ancient geography's shifting coast, and the councils' attendance lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamatha:
Syria's Hamath, a titular see suffragan of Apamea, was capital of a Canaanite kingdom whose king Thou congratulated David on beating the king of Zobah. Solomon seems to have held it, Amos calls it Hamath the Great. Assyria seized it in the seventh century before Christ, while Macedonian rulers renamed it Epiphania for Antiochus Epiphanes.

As Epiphania it is best known in church records, with nine Greek bishops listed by Lequien, the first signing at Nicaea. Arabs took it in 639 and restored the old name as Hamah. Franks held it briefly in the twelfth century, the geographer Yakout was born there, and modern Hamah on the Orontes counts 45,000 people, about 10,000 of them Christians of several rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hroswitha:
Hroswitha, also spelled Roswitha and Hrotsvitha, was a celebrated nun-poetess of the tenth century, probably born between 930 and 940 and dead about 1002. Her name, read as mighty voice, explains her titles as the mighty voice and the Nightingale of Gandersheim. Probably of aristocratic birth, she entered Gandersheim convent in her earliest youth, then famed for asceticism and learning.

Her talents found wise cultivation under her teacher Rikkardis and then under Gerberg, Otto I's niece, and the most accomplished woman of her day, later her abbess. Gerberg fostered Hroswitha's muse in hopes of adding to God's glory. Little more is known of her outer life, but her writings, the first German poetess's work, are far better known, and the entry surveys them in detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maspha:
Maspha is the name of several biblical places, from Hebrew Mitzpeh and Mitzpah, meaning watch-tower, from the root watch or observe. The Septuagint writes Maspha, Massepha, and Massephat, the Vulgate Maspha and Masphath. It fits towns in commanding positions, like Crusading Belvoir, and almost always carries the article.

Maspha of Gilead is where Jacob, ratifying his compact with Laban, set up a stone pillar and called for stones, and where Israel later gathered against Ammon. Whether it matches Ramath ha-Mitzpeh or Ramoth Gilead cannot be decided. Maspha of Benjamin, assigned by Joshua, draws rival identifications: Nebi Samwil, Shafat by Guerin, Tell en-Nasbeh, and el-Bireh, judged perhaps best for water, northerly position, and road. Maspha of Judah lies in the Shephelah between Delea and Jechtel. Near Hermon lies a Land of Maspha, and David fled with his parents to Maspha of Moab from Adullam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moses-bar-kep:
Moses Bar Kepha, one of the most celebrated Jacobite bishops and writers of the ninth century, was born at Balad about 813. He died at ninety in 903. An anonymous Syriac biography survives in a Vatican manuscript, excerpted by Assemani. It tells how he became a monk, then bishop of Beth-Ramman, Beth-Kionaya and Mossoul on the Tigris under the name Severus. For ten years he served as patriarchal visitor of Tagrit.

His numerous works span theology, philosophy, controversy, exegesis and liturgy. The chief ones are a commentary on both Testaments often quoted by Bar Hebraeus, a treatise on predestination and free will in the British Museum, and a commentary on Aristotle's Dialectics. They include a five-book Hexameron at Paris, a Tractatus de Paradiso, and writings on the soul and the sacraments. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Sergius near his native city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-omaha:
Omaha, a Nebraska diocese covering all the state north of the South Platte, spans 52,996 square miles. Jesuits visited Nebraska Indians from about 1838, the Holy See carved the Rocky Mountain vicariate from Saint Louis in 1851, and Nebraska became its own vicariate in 1857.

James O'Gorman, a Trappist from Tipperary who helped found New Melleray in Iowa, became first resident vicar apostolic in 1859. The entry follows the diocese through railroads, farming towns, and immigrant parishes to its schools, hospitals, and clergy at the century's turn. James O’Gorman took the Trappist habit at Mount Melleray in 1839 and was ordained in 1843.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ramatha: The Roman Curia suppressed Ramatha, a titular see in Palestine, in 1884. It was never a bishop's see in the proper sense. In the Middle Ages the crusaders set up the Diocese of Lydda and Rama. Its titular was generally called Bishop of Rama, meaning Ramlet, a town near Lydda but more populous than Lydda itself. Later that history was forgotten, and separate titular sees of Lydda and of Rama, or Ramatha, came into being. The mistake has since been discovered and put right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-maelrub:
Maelrubha, abbot and martyr and founder of Abercrossan, was born in 642 and died on 21 April 722. Descended from Niall, king of Ireland, through his father Elganach, he was born in County Derry and educated at Bangor. At thirty he sailed from Ireland to Scotland with monks, travelled for two years, chiefly in Argyll, and founded about half a dozen churches.

He then settled at Abercrossan, now Applecross, in the west of Ross, and built his chief church and monastery among the Picts. From there he journeyed west to Skye and Lewis, east to Forres and Keith, and north to Loch Shin, Durness, and Farr. On the journey he was martyred by Danish vikings, probably at Teampull, nine miles up Strath-Naver from Farr, and buried near the River Naver beneath a rough cross-marked stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxe-coburg-a:
Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, a Saxon-Thuringian duchy pair, covers 751 square miles: Coburg at 216 and Gotha at 541, split by Saxe-Meiningen and a Prussian strip. In 1910 the land held 257,208 people, with 3,897 Catholics, about two per cent, in 1905. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a union that kept its halves apart.

Joined in 1826, the two duchies still kept separate constitutions, diets, and internal rule, even for religion and schools, meeting jointly only for specified business. Besides the split itself, race kept them apart: Gotha's people were Saxon stock, Coburg's Frankish. Crown-land differences also shaped taxation. The entry traces both duchies from the Wettin divisions to their modern constitutional life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sodom-and-gom:
Sodom was a city of Pentapolis, joined with Gomorrha, Adama, Seboim, and Bala, later called Segor. The five cities stood in the country about the Jordan, though their exact location is unknown. Josephus placed Segor at the south end of the Dead Sea, while later scholars proposed sites north and south of the sea and on the Lisan peninsula.

For the unnatural sins of their inhabitants, Sodom, Gomorrha, Adama, and Seboim were destroyed by brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven. Since then their names stand for impenitent sin, and their fall for a proverbial display of God's just wrath. The Septuagint's word katastrophe probably bred the mistaken idea that the destruction brought great upheavals of earth and even formed the Dead Sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agatha:
St. Agatha ranks among the most venerated virgin martyrs of Christian antiquity, put to death at Catania in Sicily for steadfast profession of faith. This entry admits uncertainty over which persecution claimed her. While accepting as probably rooted in ancient tradition the later legendary life that places her martyrdom under Decius between 250 and 253.

Historic certitude, it stresses, attaches only to the martyrdom itself and to public veneration from primitive times. The Hieronymian Martyrology and the fifth- or sixth-century Carthaginian Martyrology both record her on 5 February. And by the sixth century Venantius Fortunatus was already praising her among celebrated Christian virgins, a fame the entry traces to its earliest sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hereswitha:
Hereswitha, sister of Hilda of Whitby, became a nun at Chelles after her husband fell in battle. Daughter of Hereric and Beorhtswith, she married Aethelhere, king of East Anglia, and bore him two sons, Aldwulf and Alfwold. The Liber Eliensis wrongly calls her wife of Anna, Aethelhere's elder brother, a mistake the entry corrects firmly. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places her widowhood at the battle of Winwaed in 655.

After her husband's death she entered Chelles abbey, then in the Paris diocese, and remained there until her life's end. Her feast wanders through the calendars: Stanton gives 3 September, the second English Martyrology 20 September, the first edition and Ferrari 23 September, Bucelinus 1 December. The Bollandists propose discussing her cult on that December day. The entry preserves a queen turned nun, dated four ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martha:
Martha of Bethany, sister of Mary and Lazarus, appears in Luke and John in strikingly similar portraits. Luke 10:38-42 and John 11 and 12 alone mention her, her Aramaic name appears in a Nabataean inscription from Puteoli, now in Naples Museum, dated A.D. 5, and in a Palmyrene inscription of A.D. 179, where Greek gives Marthein. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 weighs the Gospels' geography with care.

John places Mary, Martha, and Lazarus at Bethania, while Luke seems to imply they lived at one time in Galilee, though he names no town. That town may have been Magdala, which, supposing Mary of Bethania and Mary Magdalene the same person, would explain the name Magdalene. John 11:1 seems to suggest the family had moved, and Luke may have displaced his chapter 10 incident. The likeness between Luke's and John's Martha is, the entry says, very remarkable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tryphon-respi:
Martyrs whose feast the Latin Church observes on 10 November. Tryphon, said to have been born at Kampsade in Phrygia, tended geese as a boy. During the Decian persecution he was taken to Nicaea about 250 and put to death after converting the heathen prefect Licius, though fabulous stories are woven into his legend.

He is patron of gardeners in the Greek Church, which keeps his feast on 1 February. About 1005 the monk Theodoric of Fleury made Respicius his companion in story. The relics of both, with those of the Palermo virgin Nympha, were kept at Rome's Hospital of the Holy Ghost until Pius V moved them to Saint Augustine's in 1566. Leo VI, the Philosopher, delivered a eulogy upon Tryphon, and the Greek Church counts him patron of gardeners.
deuterocanonical-books-of-the-bible-apoc:
The hosted text gathers the deuterocanonical books, called the Apocrypha in English Bibles. It uses the classic English long printed with the King James Bible. The books include the two books of Esdras, Tobit, and Judith. They also include the Greek additions to Esther, the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and Baruch. The Letter of Jeremiah follows. So do the Song of the Three Holy Children, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, and the Prayer of Manasses. Both books of the Maccabees close the set.

These writings come from the last centuries before Christ. They were written in the Jewish world under Greek and Roman rule. Catholic and Orthodox churches count most of them as scripture. Most Protestant churches do not, but print them for study. Tobit's angel tale, Judith's daring rescue, and the Maccabees' revolt remain the most read.
doe-osti-17030342-implementation-of-cont: Teaching a blast code how materials break got its DOE report, and this text adds damage models to xRAGE. The pages log the coding work. The physicists get their upgrade. The breakage was modeled. The work was logged. The models were damage.

doe-osti-2588164-on-the-cfl-limit-for-st: The CFL stability limit got its math, and this DOE report covers the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The pages detail the analysis. The applied mathematicians get their result. The equation was HJB. The stability was CFL. The mathematicians got results.

The energy folks get their data. The cooperative was research. The data were energy. The feedstocks were biogas. The co-products were characterization.

The transport was charged particle. The data were physicist. The ICF were simulations. The charged were particle.
dutt-harivamsha:
Dutt's prose English Harivamsha appeared in 1897 as the Mahabharata's supplement. Harivamsha means the lineage of Hari, a name of Vishnu as Krishna. The work tells Krishna's full story, from birth to the age's dark close.

Readers follow the cowherd boy's pranks, feats, and loves in Vrindavan. His kingship, wars, and the fall of his kin fill later chapters. The supplement rounds out the great epic's most loved god's tale. Genealogy and myth blend in a warm, storyteller's flow throughout. Dutt gives the full work in faithful, complete English prose for his readers. Krishna's charm and the epic's sweep meet happily in its pages.
govdocs-archive_org-masters-mahan-compan: Companion materials for The Masters Mahan podcast make up this file, with no author named. The texts cover the show's recurring themes: a foundational conflict behind world events, a claimed depopulation agenda, and esoteric readings of mythology. Written for listeners rather than newcomers, the materials assume familiarity with the episodes they accompany. They are kept as a supplement for the show's audience and for readers tracing its ideas in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TobiasRichardMo:
Richard Tobias studied the autopsy photographs from President Kennedy's post-mortem examination and reached a stark conclusion. His monograph argues, on ballistic grounds, that four shots came from the front. That claim runs against the Warren Commission, which placed the shots behind the president.

Tobias builds his case from the photographs themselves, treating wounds and angles as physical evidence a reader can check. Works like this one kept the forensic debate alive outside official channels. For students of the assassination, it is a clear example of how independent researchers used the medical record to challenge the government's account.
mary-cary-frequently-martha:
Kate Langley Bosher wrote Mary Cary, called Frequently Martha in its short title. Harper held the rights in 1910, and Grosset and Dunlap sold this copy. The first chapter names Mary an unthankful orphan.

Miss Katherine comes in chapter two, and Mary's work starts in chapter eight. A ball, a search for truth, and a true wonder fill the mid part. The book ends with hurt, joy, and a real wedding for its young heroine. The two names hint at Mary's split moods and sharp tongue. Her orphan's view gives the tale its bite as well as its heart.
nasa-tm-19690010247-electron-mobility-in:
Harold E. Neustadter studied electron mobility among randomly located hard-core scatterers in this doctoral dissertation. He submitted it at Case Western Reserve University in June 1969. Mobility measures how freely electrons drift through a material whose atoms block and scatter them. The problem touches basic physics, with cold helium gas as one test case.

Neustadter applies Kubo's quantum statistics of irreversible processes to the drift problem. His theory recovers the known semiclassical answers where gas is hot and thin. In colder, denser gas it matches, in shape, the odd drop in mobility that Levine and Sanders measured in cold helium. He states plainly that the numbers still do not agree, so further work is needed.
podcast-tuckercarlson-T0DE7JWI5hA:
Lawyer Bob Amsterdam has represented exiled clients against authoritarian governments for decades, and more recently the Ukrainian Orthodox Church against Kyiv. With Tucker Carlson, he argues that the American aid agency USAID helps President Zelensky destroy Christianity in Ukraine using fake churches and violence, as the episode frames it.

Amsterdam presents cases of seized churches and prosecuted clergy as a persecution campaign funded from Washington. Kyiv answers that the targeted church answers to Moscow and shelters its war. Both framings cannot be wholly right, and the episode gives only Amsterdam's, at length, as advocacy. It is preserved because the church war inside Ukraine's war deserves a hearing in its dissenting form. Listeners can weigh a veteran human rights lawyer's brief against the security case he opposes.
sign-language-among-north-american-india:
The Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology, under director J. W. Powell, issued this study of sign language among North American Indians. A transcriber's note explains marks used for special sounds in the text. Verses on actors' gestures, loosely quoted from Churchill's Rosciad, also get a correction in that note.

Plains peoples could hold full talk by signs across tongues that shared no spoken words. The study sets that gesture speech beside deaf sign systems and stage gesture. Early American ethnology here records, with care, a silent language of great reach and grace that spoken-language study had long slighted.
sketches-from-my-life-by-the-late-admira:
Admiral Hobart Pasha left these sketches of his life, issued by Longmans in London in a third edition of 1887. A preface states that the pages were the last he ever wrote. Friends had urged him to record his sporting adventures, and the plan grew into a full life told by himself.

Part of the book was dictated at the Riviera during his final illness, and the whole stands rough and loosely joined, the preface grants. Friends who shared his adventures will value it most, the editor holds. A brave, genial sailor of fortune speaks here from the edge of death.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-24-canticle-:
Canticle of Canticles, in a form of Douay-Rheims translated from Latin Vulgate wording and revised by Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Behind the wording stand printings at Douay in 1609 and 1610 and at Rheims in 1582. An introduction links its spouse imagery to Christ and, in Catholic reading, to the blessed virgin mother.

Chapter one is headed as the spouse aspiring to union with Christ, in mutual love. The first line asks for the kiss of his mouth and praises love above wine. Song, desire, and praise fill a short book unlike the histories around it. Annotations direct readers past a surface love song toward a spiritual sense, which this edition makes explicit from the start.
the-house-of-martha: Frank R. Stockton wrote this novel. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published it in 1891. Their offices were in Boston and New York. Only the opening pages and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The narrator is shaped by his grandmother. A year in Europe also marks him. Later headings grow stranger. One chapter concerns the modern use of the human ear. Another covers gaining a listener. Still others mention an under-study and a plan of seclusion. A nun and a friend named Vespa appear.
the-song-of-hiawatha:
Henry W. Longfellow's long poem follows the Ojibway hero Hiawatha through twenty-two sections, from The Peace-Pipe and his childhood to his fasting, sailing, fishing, wooing, wedding feast, and final departure. An introductory note explains the poem's sources before the narrative begins.

That note credits Henry Rowe Schoolcraft with collecting the legends of many North American tribes. Schoolcraft, a historian and explorer, served as superintendent of Indian affairs for Michigan from 1836 to 1841. The Ojibway of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota supplied most of the material. Schoolcraft's marriage into an Ojibway family, traced in the note, connects the poem to the Johnston household at the heart of that collecting work.
the-woman-ayisha:
Talbot Mundy's The Woman Ayisha, dated 1922 on its opening page, drops readers into chapter six in mid-adventure. News races through a camp after men return with a prisoner. They had been sent up to Grim while the narrator searched Jael's tent. Ayisha's story has thrilled the men who heard it. Her tale promises chances for intrigue and counter-intrigue.

The men trust Grim's genius for such plots. Mundy writes fast-moving adventure set in distant lands. Loyalties shift and schemes multiply around Ayisha. Readers meet the tale already in motion, with danger close by. The chapter title threatens violence against a man named Yussuf.
three-years-in-tristan-da-cunha:
K. M. Barrow, wife of the Rev. J. G. Barrow, a missionary clergyman, wrote about three years on Tristan da Cunha. Her book carries thirty-seven illustrations from photographs and a map. She states her aim plainly in a note to readers.

Barrow wants a simple, true description of daily life in a tiny community cut off from the world. Her language comes from letters to a sister and from her journal, with help from an official Blue Book. Readers get remote island life observed by a missionary's fellow worker, including photographs by Casper Keytel of Cape Town.
